CHAPTER 4 · LEARNING AREA 4 · MAY

Presenting data

How does your class get to school? How fast does a sunflower grow? Numbers alone show this only with effort. A good chart shows it at a glance. You learn which chart fits which data, how to create it with a spreadsheet and which tricks sometimes make charts in newspapers and on the internet promise more than the numbers give.

4 LESSONS2 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • draw and read bar charts, line graphs and pie charts
  • choose the right chart for given data
  • create charts with a spreadsheet and label them correctly
  • check charts from the media critically

25%

10 mm

UNIT 12 LESSONS

1The right chart

For the way to school there are groups without an order: on foot, by bike, by bus, by car. For the temperature there is time, which runs on. These data are different, and that is why different charts suit them.

KEY POINT · THREE CHARTS

Bar chart: for comparing the values of different groups. All the bars the same width, the axis starts at 0.

Line graph: shows how a value changes over time. You may join up the points if there are values in between.

Pie chart: shows parts of a whole. The angle is the proportion times 360°.

Every chart needs a title, labelled axes with units and a note of where the data come from.

Spreadsheet: Enter the data in two columns, select both columns, insert a chart, choose the type, label the title and the axes.

Horizontal bar chart: a bar chart lying on its side. Practical with long names.

INTERACTIVE · ONE SURVEY, THREE CHARTS

Switch the type of chart and change the values. Which representation fits, which does not?

INTERACTIVE · A TIME SERIES
EXAMPLE 1 · THE WAY TO SCHOOL

In a class, 6 come on foot, 9 by bike, 8 by bus or train and 5 by car. Which chart fits?

For comparing, a bar chart; for the proportions, a pie chart: the bike has $\tfrac{9}{28} \approx 32\%$, so about $116^\circ$.

A line graph does not fit: the groups have no order.

EXAMPLE 2 · THE SUNFLOWER

A sunflower is measured every week: 8, 15, 27, 44, 70, 98, 125, 140 cm. In which week does it grow most?

A line graph shows it: the line is steepest between week 5 and 6 (28 cm), almost as steep between week 6 and 7 (27 cm).

It grows most from week 5 to week 6: 28 cm.

EXERCISES

Which chart fits? a) the population of a town from 2000 to 2025   b) votes in the election for class representative   c) what pocket money is spent on   d) favourite subjects of classes 7a and 7b compared

a) line graph   b) bar chart or pie chart   c) pie chart   d) bar chart with two bars side by side each time

Pets in a class: dog 8, cat 6, fish 3, none 11. Draw a bar chart with a title and a labelled axis.

Four bars of the same width, axis from 0 to 12. Title for example: “Pets in class 7b (28 answers)”.

Temperatures during one day: 8 am 4 °C, 10 am 7 °C, 12 noon 11 °C, 2 pm 13 °C, 4 pm 10 °C, 6 pm 6 °C. Draw a line graph. When was it warmest, and when did the temperature rise most?

Warmest at 2 pm. It rose most between 10 am and 12 noon, by 4 degrees.

Out of €20 pocket money, Mia spends €5 on sweets, saves €8, spends €4 on leisure and €3 on other things. Calculate the angles and draw a pie chart.

25% → 90°, 40% → 144°, 20% → 72°, 15% → 54°. Check: 360°.

Describe step by step how you turn the table from exercise 2 into a bar chart with a spreadsheet. What do you still have to add by hand afterwards?

Enter the animals in column A and the numbers in column B, select both columns, insert a chart, choose bars. Then add the title, the axis label (“Number”) and the source, and check whether the axis starts at 0.

TEST YOURSELF!

Which angle belongs to 20%?

$0.2 \cdot 360^\circ = 72^\circ$

Which chart best shows how a value changes over time?

The line graph.

5 out of 20 people asked cycle. What percentage is that?

25%

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Charts in the media

An advert shows two bars: the bar of the company’s own product is twice as high as the other one. Only at second glance do you see: the axis does not start at 0 but at 400. In reality the difference is tiny.

KEY POINT · QUESTIONS TO CHECK CHARTS
  1. Does the axis start at 0? Are the steps on the axis equal?
  2. Are lengths being compared, or pictures whose area grows as well?
  3. Which period of time is shown? Is something missing before or after it?
  4. Are they absolute numbers or percentages? And a percentage of what?
  5. Where do the data come from, and how many people were asked?

Picture symbols: If a picture becomes twice as high and twice as wide, it has four times the area. It looks four times as big, although the value is only twice as big.

INTERACTIVE · TWO TRICKS
EXAMPLE 3 · THE CUT-OFF AXIS

Company A sells 410 bikes, company B 420. In the chart the axis starts at 400. How big does the difference look, and how big is it?

In the picture A’s bar is 10 high, B’s 20: B looks twice as big.

In reality B sells only 10 bikes more; that is about 2.4%.

EXAMPLE 4 · A PERCENTAGE OF WHAT?

A headline: “E-scooter accidents up 50%!” There were 20 the year before. How many are there now?

$1.5 \cdot 20 = 30$. There are 10 more accidents.

50% sounds a lot. Only the base value tells you whether it really is a lot.

EXERCISES

A chart shows the values 90 and 100. The axis starts at 80. How many times as high does the second bar look? By what percentage is the value really bigger?

In the picture: 10 and 20, so twice as high. Really: $\tfrac{10}{90} \approx 11\%$ bigger.

A picture symbol (a bottle) is meant to show that three times as much is drunk. The second bottle is three times as high and three times as wide. What impression does that make?

Its area is $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ times as big. It looks nine times as big, not three times.

A line graph shows the number of visitors to an open-air pool for the two hottest weeks only. What is misleading about it if you draw conclusions about the whole summer?

The extract is not typical. For the whole summer you would have to show all the weeks, including the cool ones.

For the values 52, 54, 55 and 57 (points in four tests), draw an honest bar chart and one that fakes a big improvement.

Honest: axis from 0, the bars are almost the same height. Exaggerating: axis from 50, the last bar looks three and a half times as high as the first.

A survey: “90% are satisfied with our product!” 10 people were asked at the company’s stand. Evaluate the statement with the checking questions.

9 out of 10 people are very few. At the company’s stand there are mostly people who like the product. The statement cannot be applied to everyone.

TEST YOURSELF!

A value rises from 400 to 420. By what percentage?

$\tfrac{20}{400} = 5\%$

A picture becomes twice as high and twice as wide. How many times as big is its area?

4 times

Values 410 and 420, axis from 400. How many times as high does the second bar look?

20 instead of 10: twice as high.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A pie chart has four parts with 90°, 120°, 60° and 90°. What percentage is each part?

25%, about 33.3%, about 16.7% and 25%.

Connecting with chapter 2.4: The proportion of cyclists in a town rose from 12% to 15%. One article says “+3%”, another “+25%”. Who is right?

The two mean different things: there are 3 percentage points more, and $\tfrac{3}{12} = 25\%$ more. “+3%” is worded wrongly; correct would be “+3 percentage points”.

Connecting with chapter 2.2: The lowest temperatures of one week: −2, −5, 1, 3, −1, −4, 0 °C. Draw a line graph with an axis that also has negative values.

The axis goes, for example, from −6 to 4 °C. The line lies partly below and partly above the zero line. Coldest day: the second one with −5 °C.

Look on the internet for a chart with current data, for example from the state statistical office. Check it with the five checking questions and present it to the class.

Individual answers. Pay attention to the title, axes, units, period of time, base value and source.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

William Playfair, the inventor of charts

For a long time numbers stood only in tables. The Scotsman William Playfair (1759 to 1823) changed that. In his book The Commercial and Political Atlas of 1786 he showed England’s trade with other countries as line graphs, year by year. For Scotland he was missing the figures for several years. So he drew the values of a single year as bars next to each other: the first bar chart.

In 1801 his Statistical Breviary appeared. In it a circle shows how large the territories of the Ottoman Empire in Europe, Asia and Africa were: the first pie chart. Playfair even coloured the pieces in different colours.

Sources: W. Playfair, The Commercial and Political Atlas, London 1786. W. Playfair, The Statistical Breviary, London 1801.
